newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt discount rate cut first of many - bankers.
newsitem.headline: Egypt discount rate cut first of many - bankers.

text.p: A recent discount rate cut by the Central Bank of Egypt is likely to put a brake on the pound's strength and boost direct investment, bankers say.

The central bank cut the rate last Thursday by 0.50 percentage point to 12.25 percent. Although bankers say they never borrow at the discount rate, it indicates the central bank's intention about interest rates in general.
The reduction has taken the benchmark rate down by one percentage point in the past five months and bankers expect the downtrend to continue in response to market conditions.
"The central bank is trying to protect the pound against appreciation," one banker said.
"The large inflows of capital that have been coming in recently have created a lot of demand for the pound but the government wants to see it lower to boost exports," she said.
Investment-grade credit ratings by Standard and Poor's, accelerated reforms and a huge marketing drive have drawn investors to the Egyptian economy in the past year.

Minister of State for Economic Affairs Youssef Boutros-Ghali said last week foreign direct investment in 1996 was between $800 and $900 million and that he expected it to grow to $1.5 billion in 1997. The pound, whose rate against the dollar has been stable at around 3.4 pounds for years, has also strengthened in recent weeks.

Bankers say that current interest rates on pound loans, which range between 11 and 13 percent, do not encourage investors. Some say the cut is an attempt by the central bank to drive the rates lower and stimulate direct investment.
"The reasonable level is around nine to 10 percent for borrowers," one banker said.
"This trend will continue until interest rates are at a maximum of about 8.5 to nine percent," another banker said.
The cut also follows lower yield rates on treasury bills and reduced inflation, bankers say.
Others say the secretive central bank wants to issue bonds whose yields are related to the t-bills and that it would benefit from a low payout.

T-bill yields have been gradually declining, and since November 1995 have fallen to an average of 9.049 percent from about 10.5 percent for 91-day bills, the lowest level since their introduction in 1991.

The average yield for 182-day bills broke the nine-percent level in Monday's auction and fell to 8.950 percent while inflation fell to 5.4 percent in the year to the end of February from 6.3 percent a year earlier.
While some bankers say the pound can stand further rate cuts, others fear that if rates fall too much, investors will switch their pounds into the more stable U.S. currency.
"When they (interest rates) are less than 7.5 to eight percent, dollarisation can take place," one banker said.
Interest rates on Egyptian pound short-term deposits, which hover around 10 percent, are more profitable than dollar deposits which yield about six percent.
But other bankers say that with the economy gaining a good reputation, dollarisation is unlikely to set in.

"The Central Bank can do it. It has nothing to worry about now with foreigners having strong confidence in the economy," a banker said. "There is no panic from declining interest rates on the Egyptian pound...The Egyptian economy has already passed over the confidence-building stage."
$1 = 3.395 pounds
